The retail giant is frequently part of Gemini’s shopping advice, yet its website is completely absent from the sources supporting those recommendations. That creates an unusual disconnect between brand recognition and the ability to capture discovery traffic.

A Semrush AI Visibility Index study found that Gemini mentioned Amazon in 40.5% of tracked holiday shopping prompts in September 2026, more than any other retailer. Yet amazon.com appeared in none of the Gemini answers as a cited source.
Amazon’s Visibility Comes With a Catch
The gap is particularly striking when compared with other major retailers.

Semrush points to Amazon’s robots.txt configuration as a likely explanation. The file blocks Google-Extended, a crawler that allows website owners to control whether their content is used for Gemini training and grounding. By blocking it, Amazon restricts Gemini’s access to its website content for these purposes.

This does not mean Amazon has disappeared from Google’s broader search ecosystem. The study found that Google AI Overviews cited amazon.com in 11.4% of holiday prompts, while Google AI Mode did so in 5.3%. The exclusion is specific to Gemini.

For Amazon, the strategy could reflect a deliberate preference to keep shoppers inside its own ecosystem rather than make its product pages and pricing information available to an external AI assistant.
The more consequential part of the finding is where Gemini turns instead.
Among the 506 Gemini answers that mentioned Amazon, blackfriday.com was the most frequently cited source, appearing in 26.3%. Walmart was cited in 8.9%, Best Buy in 7.1% and Target in 5.9%.

In other words, Gemini can recommend Amazon while relying on other websites to support its answers. That gives deal aggregators and competing retailers an opportunity to occupy the source links accompanying shopping recommendations.
The distinction between mentions and citations is increasingly important for retailers. Being named keeps a brand in the conversation; being cited gives shoppers a direct source to explore.

Amazon’s approach also carries a potential trade-off. Restricting access may protect its control over product information, but it could limit how much visibility its own website receives within an increasingly influential AI discovery channel.

Amazon investors should watch whether AI shopping assistants become meaningful sources of product discovery and referral traffic. The company’s enormous customer base and established shopping app give it reasons to believe consumers will find their way to Amazon independently.
But if Gemini and other AI platforms become increasingly important shopping gateways, keeping the website outside their citation ecosystem could become a competitive disadvantage.

title: Google’s Amazon Blind Spot: Gemini Recommends It More Than Any Retailer, But Never Links to It
